title: Blanche's AG nomination advances after he rescinds the $1.8B "anti-weaponization fund"
summary: The Senate Judiciary Committee advanced acting AG Todd Blanche 12–10 on party lines after he issued written orders rescinding a $1.8 billion fund created in Trump's IRS settlement and narrowing the scope of the Trump family's audit immunity. Republican holdouts Cornyn and Tillis called it settled; Susan Collins then said she'd vote no. Every outlet checked — including Fox — reported that the orders don't legally prevent the fund's revival, which makes this a useful test of how differently outlets weight the same conceded fact.

outlets.name: Fox News
outlets.framing: Led on Collins's defection as a threat to the confirmation math and to Thune's plan to confirm Blanche before the August recess. Described the Cornyn–Tillis deal as giving "explicit direction that the anti-weaponization fund was dead." Worth noting for the comparison: Fox's own news copy also reported that "critics of the deal in the Senate say there's no real binding mechanism" preventing Trump or Blanche from tearing it up after confirmation — the same limitation the left-leaning outlets emphasized.

outlets.name: Washington Examiner
outlets.framing: Procedural framing throughout — the vote as a "crucial procedural hurdle" cleared before recess. Gave the most detailed account of what Blanche's order actually says (no members appointed, no money transferred, no claims paid) and of the audit clarification's limits. Ran the Democratic objections at length and in their own words, quoting Booker's "all hat and no cattle" and Blumenthal calling the documents "a sham," without rebutting them.

outlets.name: CBS News
outlets.framing: The most complete documentary account of the deal itself, quoting the DOJ order, the senators' joint statement, and Cornyn's "stake driven through the heart" line. Closed the loop with the single most load-bearing sentence in the coverage: "The written settlement reached with Mr. Trump and his lawyers has not been modified." Also carried Trump saying the same day that he still views the fund as "a positive" and that he didn't know what had been agreed to.

outlets.name: AP (via PBS NewsHour)
outlets.framing: Balanced the two competing readings against each other rather than picking one: Grassley saying the rescission "put this issue to bed once and for all," against Durbin saying the fund "can easily be revived with a new order from the Department of Justice 15 minutes after Mr. Blanche is confirmed." Added a checkable finding neither senator raised — that the order doesn't stop the administration from compensating the same people through a pre-existing damages-claim process. Also laid out the floor math (McConnell absent, Murkowski and Cassidy undeclared).

outlets.name: ABC News
outlets.framing: Straight floor-and-committee account organized around Collins's announcement. Stated the loophole as flat fact in its own voice — "the agreement reached has no language preventing the resurrection of the controversial fund under a different name or method" — and then immediately gave Cornyn his answer to it. Ran Tillis's "payout pot for punks" line and Booker's and Whitehouse's objections at similar length.

outlets.name: NPR
outlets.framing: The sharpest characterization of the group, delivered as reporter analysis on Morning Edition: the two Blanche documents "purport to" do what they claim, and "legal experts say neither document… is actually legally binding." Went further than the news accounts by noting the tax-immunity benefits "still very much remain in place," and then widened out to Blanche's broader record — Epstein files, the Comey indictment, judges questioning DOJ representations — which the other outlets mostly left out of the vote story.

synthesis.label: Consistent across all 6:
synthesis.text: The committee voted 12–10 on party lines on Aug. 4. Blanche issued written orders Aug. 2–3 rescinding the $1.8 billion fund and narrowing the audit immunity to Trump, two sons, the Trump Organization, and already-filed returns. Cornyn and Tillis flipped to yes; Collins announced she'd vote no. The underlying IRS settlement with Trump was not itself modified. No outlet disputes any of this.

synthesis.label: Where it splits — and where it notably doesn't:
synthesis.text: The central contested question is whether the rescission is binding. This is a rare case where the answer isn't split by lean: Fox reported Senate critics saying there's "no real binding mechanism," ABC stated in its own voice that the agreement has no language preventing revival, AP flagged an alternate compensation route that survives the order, and NPR cited legal experts saying neither document is legally binding. That convergence makes it a reporting finding rather than a partisan characterization. What differs is placement: for Fox and the Examiner it's a paragraph inside a procedural story; for NPR it's the thesis.

synthesis.label: Framing among outlets that agree on the facts:
synthesis.text: Fox and the Examiner organized around process and vote-counting. CBS and AP organized around the documents themselves and let Grassley and Durbin argue in their own quotes. ABC organized around Collins. NPR was alone in going past the vote to Blanche's broader DOJ record, which is a genuine editorial choice about scope rather than a factual disagreement — the vote story and the fitness story are not the same story, and reasonable desks put that material in different places.

synthesis.label: Gap in this pass:
synthesis.text: Checked 6 outlets. Missing coverage that was located but could not be retrieved: CNN's "major loopholes" piece, NBC News, CNBC, Washington Post, Washington Times, The Federalist, MS NOW. The Federalist in particular would be a useful second right-side data point. Also unchecked: Reuters, WSJ, NYT, Bloomberg, Newsweek, The Hill.

title: Trump calls off Iran strikes, says talks are underway — Tehran says they aren't
summary: Trump canceled what he described as the largest planned U.S. attack since World War II, saying Gulf allies and Iran had asked for time and that the "perimeters of a deal" to reopen the Strait of Hormuz were in place. Iran's foreign ministry then said it is not negotiating with the United States at all — only with Oman, over a temporary shipping route. This is a factual dispute, not just a framing one, and outlets split on how prominently they surfaced it.

outlets.name: Fox News
outlets.framing: Live-blog coverage led with the administration's account: a deal is "imminent," the canceled strike would have been the largest since World War II, and Iran has agreed to an "immediate, complete, and total opening" of the strait. Oil falling more than $5 a barrel was treated as the confirming evidence. Fox did carry Iran's foreign minister saying the Iran–Oman talks were in their final stages, but did not foreground the gap between "Iran–Oman talks" and Trump's claim of U.S.–Iran talks.

outlets.name: Reuters (via Spokesman-Review)
outlets.framing: Original reporting that cuts hardest against the announcement: a senior Iranian source and two regional officials told Reuters the deal actually on the table would give Tehran control over ships entering the Gulf — "one of the biggest concessions yet to Iran" — and those same sources "pushed back against assertions by U.S. President Donald Trump that a deal reopening the strait was imminent." Reuters also reported the U.S. Army has used up nearly all of its long-range precision missiles, and noted Washington had no immediate reply on the proposed terms.

outlets.name: Bloomberg (via Spokesman-Review)
outlets.framing: Straight market-and-diplomacy account that stated the discrepancy plainly without editorializing: Trump said talks with Iran would begin Monday, and "there's as yet no clarity on what level of talks he was referring to or who would lead them." Added its own reporting that the Hormuz middle passage under discussion has been mined by Iran and may need clearing before regular use. Quoted the Iranian spokesman directly: "We are not currently negotiating with the United States."

outlets.name: AP (via PBS NewsHour)
outlets.framing: Rather than covering the cancellation as news, AP built a checkable timeline of every prior announcement — April 7, April 21, May 18, June 11, June 17, July 7, July 27, Aug. 1 — showing that each announced halt was "upended by renewed attacks days or even hours afterward." The framing is not that Trump is wrong about this one, but that the pattern is the story. Documentary and verifiable rather than adjectival.

outlets.name: PolitiFact (via PBS NewsHour)
outlets.framing: Directly fact-checked Trump's claim that the war is going "extremely well," concluding key stated goals — denuclearization, regime change, reopening the strait — remain unmet. Quoted named experts across the spectrum, including Carnegie's Aaron David Miller calling it "an 'incomplete'" and, if the war ended today, "a major strategic defeat by the administration's own metrics." Also supplied the hard numbers: $37.5B in direct military spending, 18 U.S. service members killed, gas about $1.15 above pre-war levels.

outlets.name: NPR
outlets.framing: Short, blunt framing built entirely around the contradiction — headline and lede both lead with Iran denying the negotiations Trump announced. Reported that Trump posted the "perimeters of a deal" had been reached and that "Iran did not confirm the statement," leaving the discrepancy stated rather than adjudicated.

outlets.name: CBS News
outlets.framing: Live-updates format that gave the administration's own spokesman the frame: Rubio saying there has "been progress made" in the Iran–Oman talks "but not finality yet." Ran Trump's harshest line ("I want to give them every last chance before decapitation") in the headline alongside it. Added a neutral status check the other outlets mostly skipped — that commercial traffic through the strait "remains murky" and both Iran and Oman claim control of the waterway.

outlets.name: Al Jazeera
outlets.framing: Notable because the piece is bylined "Al Jazeera Staff and AP" and tagged AP as its source — so the sourcing is closer to wire copy than to an Al Jazeera editorial line. Gave extended direct quotation to Trump ("Total Surrender," the "Wall of Steel" blockade, "last chance") and to the Iranian spokesman's rebuttal in roughly equal measure. Supplied regional detail absent from U.S. coverage, including Iran routing containers through Pakistani ports around the blockade.

synthesis.label: Consistent across all 8:
synthesis.text: Trump canceled a planned strike over the weekend of Aug. 1–2 and said Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Qatar and Iran had asked him to. Iran's foreign ministry publicly said it is not negotiating with the United States and that its talks are with Oman over a temporary transit route. Oil fell sharply on the news. No outlet disputes any of that.

synthesis.label: Where it splits:
synthesis.text: This one is a reporting finding, not a framing preference. Reuters spoke to a senior Iranian source and two regional officials who said the agreement actually under discussion would give Iran control over inbound traffic — the opposite of the "immediate, complete, and total opening" Trump described — and who directly disputed that a deal was imminent. Bloomberg separately reported there was no clarity on what talks Trump meant or who would lead them. Fox's news coverage relayed the administration's version and did carry the Iranian foreign minister, but framed the Iran–Oman track as evidence the deal was coming rather than as a contradiction of it.

synthesis.label: Framing among outlets that agree on the facts:
synthesis.text: AP and PolitiFact both went documentary rather than rhetorical — AP with a dated timeline of eight prior announce-then-resume cycles since February, PolitiFact with named experts and dollar figures. NPR stated the contradiction and stopped there. CBS gave the frame to Rubio's own hedge ("progress… but not finality yet"), which is arguably the most administration-sourced skeptical note available. Al Jazeera, despite the outlet's lean, ran what is substantially AP copy here.

synthesis.label: Gap in this pass:
synthesis.text: Checked 8 outlets. Only one right-leaning outlet (Fox News) — Washington Times and Washington Examiner both have same-week Iran coverage that could not be retrieved for this pass and would make the right-side comparison fairer. Also missing: CNN, NBC, Washington Post, BBC, Guardian, NYT, WSJ, Financial Times, The Economist, MS NOW, NewsNation, Deutsche Welle.

title: Trump's primetime address on "election security"
summary: White House declassified documents alongside a speech renewing 2020 election claims and pushing the SAVE America Act. Outlets agree on what happened; they split hard on whether the documents back up the claims.

outlets.name: Fox News
outlets.framing: Covered straightforwardly as an "election integrity" announcement. News coverage relayed Trump's claims (China accessed 220M voter files, intelligence was hidden from him) largely at face value; a companion opinion piece framed the claims as warranting investigation and criticized "Democratic critics" for disputing the evidence.

outlets.name: CNN
outlets.framing: Reported the declassification claims, then directly noted the documents "largely discuss vulnerabilities that have been known for years." Contrasted Trump's China-interference claim with a 2021 U.S. intelligence assessment that reached the opposite conclusion.

outlets.name: AP
outlets.framing: An AP review of the actual declassified documents found no confirmation of Trump's core claims — many pages were heavily redacted, and the material largely described vulnerabilities already publicly documented for years. Quoted an election-security expert calling the release "a dud."

outlets.name: NYT
outlets.framing: Reporter Maggie Haberman characterized several of Trump's claims in the speech as exaggerated relative to what the underlying documents actually showed, describing the documents themselves as notably more cautious in their conclusions than the speech.

outlets.name: MS NOW (fka MSNBC)
outlets.framing: Framed the speech as a rehash of long-rejected 2020 conspiracy theories, emphasizing that current and former intelligence officials said no evidence exists that any foreign country changed the outcome of the 2020 election, and noting recent leadership changes atop the intelligence community.

outlets.name: Al Jazeera
outlets.framing: Described the speech as "controversial," led with a Democratic lawmaker's response accusing Trump of trying to sow doubt about the 2026 election, and noted experts found no conclusive evidence backing his claims.

outlets.name: ABC News
outlets.framing: Relayed the speech's claims in a fairly neutral takeaways format — what Trump said, what documents he released — with comparatively less immediate pushback framing than CNN or MS NOW in the initial writeup.

outlets.name: NBC News
outlets.framing: Live-blog coverage noted plainly that Trump "has repeatedly claimed without evidence" that the 2020 election was affected by fraud, embedding that characterization directly into the news update rather than as separate analysis.

outlets.name: Time
outlets.framing: Framed the presentation as effective for Trump's base rhetorically but risky factually, previewing that the specific claims would face heavy fact-checking scrutiny in the days after.

outlets.name: Newsweek
outlets.framing: Analyzed the speech through a media-literacy lens — arguing its function was to keep the 2020 dispute "feeling unresolved" through repetition, regardless of whether the newly released documents actually supported the claims.

synthesis.label: Consistent across all 10:
synthesis.text: Trump gave the speech, declassified documents were released alongside it, and he's pushing for the SAVE America Act before the midterms. Nobody disputes these bare facts.

synthesis.label: Where it splits:
synthesis.text: Fox's news coverage and opinion content largely presented Trump's claims on their own terms. Every other outlet checked here — including the AP wire service, which has no ideological mandate — reported that a direct review of the documents did not support the central claims. That's a reporting finding, not just left-leaning framing, since AP's review is checkable against the primary documents.

synthesis.label: Framing among outlets that agree on the facts:
synthesis.text: AP and ABC stayed closest to neutral "here's what was claimed, here's what was found" language. MS NOW, Al Jazeera, and Newsweek led harder with skepticism. NBC folded "without evidence" directly into straight news copy rather than flagging it as analysis.

synthesis.label: Gap in this pass:
synthesis.text: Checked 10 of 17 outlets in the pool. Still missing: BBC, Reuters, Guardian, Washington Post, Financial Times, The Economist, Christian Science Monitor, Deutsche Welle, NewsNation, WSJ.

title: Trump imposes 50% tariffs on Canadian goods
summary: Trump signed three proclamations imposing 50% tariffs on a range of Canadian goods (autos, alcohol, dairy, and hundreds of other items), citing Canadian trade discrimination. Unlike the election speech, coverage here is fairly consistent on the facts — the split is more about emphasis than dueling narratives.

outlets.name: Fox Business
outlets.framing: Led with the administration's own framing and a direct quote from a senior official: this is not a trade war, but a defensive response to Canadian discrimination against U.S. autos, alcohol, and dairy exports.

outlets.name: NY Post
outlets.framing: Covered the broader run-up to this tariff fight, including Trump's shift in tone toward Carney personally, without heavy editorializing on whether the discrimination claims hold up.

outlets.name: CNBC
outlets.framing: Reported the legal mechanism in detail — the tariffs use a rarely-invoked 1930 law (Section 338) with no public precedent since 1949 — and noted Canadian officials pushed back, without asserting who's right on the discrimination claim itself.

outlets.name: Newsweek
outlets.framing: Straightforward explainer format: what's tariffed, what's exempt, and the administration's account that year-long talks with Canada went nowhere before this was announced.

outlets.name: Washington Post
outlets.framing: Straight news account of the announcement and its 30-day timeline, framed around the discrimination dispute without independently weighing in on the underlying trade claims.

outlets.name: CNN Business
outlets.framing: Added the most skepticism of the group: quoted an economist noting the tariffs cover only about 0.6% of total U.S. imports despite the steep headline rate, and flagged the untested legal authority being used as notable regardless of outcome.

outlets.name: The Hill
outlets.framing: Centered Canadian PM Mark Carney's response calling the move a violation of the USMCA trade agreement, giving more direct voice to the Canadian side than most U.S. coverage.

synthesis.label: Consistent across the board:
synthesis.text: All outlets checked agree on the core facts: 50% tariffs, three proclamations, a 30-day runway, and the administration's stated justification (auto/alcohol/dairy discrimination). No outlet disputed that this announcement happened as described.

synthesis.label: Where emphasis differs:
synthesis.text: Fox Business and NY Post led with the administration's rationale largely unchallenged. CNN Business was the outlet most likely to add independent context cutting against the announcement's impact (economists noting the tariffs affect a small share of total trade) and to flag the legal mechanism as untested. The Hill gave the most direct space to Canada's rebuttal.

synthesis.label: Why this is a useful contrast to the election speech story:
synthesis.text: This is what non-polarized coverage of a Trump story looks like — outlets differ in emphasis and how much independent pushback they add, but nobody is contesting the basic facts the way AP directly contested the documents in the election-speech story.

synthesis.label: Gap in this pass:
synthesis.text: Checked 7 outlets. Still missing: Guardian, BBC, Reuters, AP, Financial Times, The Economist, PBS, Christian Science Monitor, Deutsche Welle, NewsNation, WSJ, Washington Examiner, MS NOW, Al Jazeera, ABC, NBC, Time.

title: Trump says Netanyahu "will not be arrested" after Mamdani threat
summary: NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani said his administration was in "active conversation" about arresting Netanyahu (under an ICC warrant) if he visits for the UN General Assembly in September. Trump posted that Netanyahu will not be arrested "in any way, shape, or form." This is more a political-theater story than a policy dispute over facts.

outlets.name: RedState (via Fox network)
outlets.framing: Opinion-toned piece dismissing Mamdani's position outright, using pointed language ("fever dream," describing his comments as "anti-Semitic, pro-Hamas") and citing Sen. John Fetterman calling Mamdani a "clown." Clearly commentary, not a straight news account.

outlets.name: Washington Times
outlets.framing: Straight account of Trump's Truth Social post and Mamdani's underlying comments, including full quotes from both sides without much added framing.

outlets.name: CNBC
outlets.framing: Neutral rundown of the back-and-forth, including the ICC's 2024 warrant against Netanyahu and Israel's dismissal of the ICC as illegitimate, without taking a side on the underlying legal dispute.

outlets.name: The Hill
outlets.framing: Straight news framing similar to CNBC — laid out both men's statements and the ICC warrant's basis without editorializing on who has the better argument.

outlets.name: Bloomberg
outlets.framing: Concise wire-style account focused on the factual sequence — what Mamdani said, what Trump posted in response — without characterizing either side's position.

outlets.name: Al Jazeera
outlets.framing: Led with Trump's rejection of the arrest threat, included Israel's dismissal of the ICC as a "kangaroo court," and gave roughly equal space to Mamdani's original comments — mixed rather than strongly pushing back on Trump's framing here.

synthesis.label: Consistent across the board:
synthesis.text: Every outlet agrees on the sequence: Mamdani raised the idea of a possible arrest, Trump posted a forceful rejection citing Netanyahu's role against Iran, and the ICC's underlying 2024 warrant is real and undisputed as a fact of what it is (though the U.S. and Israel don't recognize the ICC's jurisdiction here).

synthesis.label: Where it splits:
synthesis.text: The clearest gap here isn't between left and right news desks — it's between straight news accounts (Washington Times, CNBC, The Hill, Bloomberg, Al Jazeera) that mostly relayed both sides' statements, and openly opinion-toned commentary (RedState) that dismissed one side outright. Worth flagging: this kind of piece sits closer to opinion journalism than to the news reporting this tracker is otherwise comparing.

synthesis.label: Notably absent so far:
synthesis.text: No outlet in this initial pass strongly challenged either man's underlying claim (that Netanyahu is protected from arrest in the U.S. vs. that the ICC warrant has real legal weight) — this looks more like a political dispute being reported on its face than a factual dispute like the election-speech story.

synthesis.label: Gap in this pass:
synthesis.text: Checked 6 outlets, and one of them (RedState) is opinion content rather than straight news — worth replacing with an actual Fox News or NY Post straight-news piece if you want a cleaner right-leaning news comparison here. Still missing most of the base pool.
